steps: Plan & permit
Check restrictions and permit needs with the local authority; plan fireplace, chimney and options together. Remove the door until all finishing is done.

Taking the door off protects it from scratches and from drywall dust, muriatic acid, plaster, cement, paint and other sprays or liquids.

If an option that needs wiring or electricity might be added later, run suitable wiring during framing; it is difficult to add afterwards. The options list on p. 29 shows which ones need it.

RSF strongly recommends installation and service by professionals certified by the National Fireplace Institute (U.S.) or Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (Canada).
Frame the enclosure
Frame to Figure 4 (a drawing). Combustibles no closer than the side, back and top standoffs; no insulation in clearance spaces; no shelves or cupboards in the enclosure above.

Pick a spot that avoids cutting roof and floor joists; no special floor reinforcement is needed. Finish all interior walls of the enclosure flat. The framing dimensions are shown only in the Figure 4 drawing, marked as larger than required for ease of installation; take them from the PDF.

Run the chimney up inside the house if possible. Outside, enclose it in an insulated chase: a cold chimney causes poor draft.

Don't pack the required air space with insulation or other materials.
Set & secure the unit
Hold the minimum ceiling clearance from the bottom of the legs (6' standard, 7' mobile home) in both the enclosure and the room. Screw the legs to the floor through the pre-cut holes.
Top standoff
Screw it to the unit top; bend the back shield to 45° along the crease. Keep a ¼" min. air gap from 2x4 framing to the back shield; nothing below the header supports.

The top standoff provides clearance to combustible framing and includes a heat shield. It must be installed, and it ships flat.

Don't fill the gap between the fireplace and the standoff with insulation or any other material; the finishing material covers it.

Nothing can be placed below the header supports of the top standoff, combustible or not. The space must remain empty.
Outside air duct
Optional unless code requires it or it's a mobile home. Fit the rotating elbow under the unit; run insulated aluminium flex rated over 200° F to a wall inlet at least 5' below the rain cap.

1. Remove the outside air cover under the fireplace (four screws, short Phillips) and break out its central part.
  2. Attach 4" aluminium duct to the elbow inlet with metal screws and aluminum tape.
  3. Strip any plastic covering so none is under the fireplace or within 3" of it; tape the insulation to the duct with aluminium tape.
  4. For a 5" run, use 4" just to clear the base, then a 4"-5" increaser (not included).
  5. Set the elbow in its support on the unit with at least two of the screws, orient it, then tighten and tape the joint.
  6. Cut a 4 ¼" hole (5 ¼" for 5" duct) in the outside wall, push the inlet in from outside and seal it.
  7. Screw the duct to the inlet sleeve, put the insulation and plastic back over it, and tape.

4" duct for a total run under 25', 5" for longer runs; max 12' vertical rise above the unit base. Make the duct long enough for a P-trap loop to avoid condensation, don't crimp it at corners, and never terminate the inlet in an attic.
Facing, trim & mantel
Cover the facing with ½" min. cement board; non-combustible finish only, no gypsum. Rivet on the chosen trim and fit the two louver pins; set any mantel per Tables 2 and 3.

Only fully non-combustible panels such as James Hardie HardieBacker® or USG Durock® cement board are acceptable. Screw them into the framing beside the fireplace or into the grey region on the fireplace (Figure 8). Drywall can't come closer than the side and top standoffs; the front face of the top standoff counts as facing. The minimum non-combustible facing is shown as a drawing (Figure 9).

A trim is mandatory: Straight Trim FO-F3600ST gives masonry or stone a straight edge to butt against; Frame Trim FO-F3600FT overlaps thin finishes that protrude ½" to 1" beyond the fireplace face. Both install with the rivets provided; unlatch the door and lift it off if needed to reach them all.

Gypsum board is considered combustible regardless of its fire rating. Never use it to cover the fireplace.
Chimney
6" ICC EXCEL only. 12" square framed openings, radiation shield at every floor, first length fixed with three screws, 2" to combustibles. Extend 3' above the roof and 2' above anything within 10'.

1. Cut and frame the openings in floors, ceilings and roof: 12" square rough opening (slightly bigger is fine, never smaller).
  2. From below, install a radiation shield at each floor; at the attic, a radiation shield and a storm collar.
  3. Fix the first chimney length to the fireplace with the three screws provided, then assemble the rest.
  4. At the roof, install the roof radiation shield (XM-6ERRS) so it extends 3" above the roof line.
  5. Flashing: vented if the chimney is enclosed to the roof, regular if not. Don't block the vented flashing's openings.
  6. Storm collar over chimney and flashing, sealed below and on top with exterior sealant (no roofing tar).
  7. Fit the rain cap and secure it tightly.

Roof brace if the chimney is more than 5' above the roof. Offsets: max 30° in the USA, 45° in Canada; max four elbows; three metal screws per joint; a roof, wall or offset support above each offset. Through an exterior wall, use an angled wall insulated radiation shield (XM-6EWRSI30 or XM-6EWRSI45).

Masonry chimney: run EXCEL chimney from the fireplace to a listed liner (ULC-S635, ULC-S640 or UL-1777) through masonry adaptor FO-FDM6, with at least one 18" EXCEL length after the elbow, and keep the EXCEL chimney at least 12" from the ceiling where it enters the masonry. An existing chimney must first be inspected by an authority having jurisdiction.
Hearth extension & spark guard
Non-combustible hearth 18" deep and 38½" wide, centered on the opening; no minimum thickness. On a combustible floor, set the provided 5" x 36" spark guard 2½" under the unit.

Use brick, tile, stone, slate or another non-combustible material. The provided spark guard goes halfway under the fireplace and halfway under the hearth extension, centered on the door opening, so sparks can't lodge there. It isn't required on a non-combustible floor.

Raised installations need a site-built guard at least 36" wide, centered on the door opening:

  • Unit 2½" or less above the hearth flooring: Z-shaped guard as tall as the gap, reaching at least 2½" under both the hearth extension and the fireplace.
  • More than 2½": right-angle guard with sides at least 2½" x 2½", covered with non-combustible material.
Mobile home extras
Outside air kit (FO-INT recommended) and the ERCS chimney-cap spark screen are required. Secure with two #8 wood screws at least 1 ½" long; never in a bedroom or sleeping room.

• Outside air avoids room air starvation, icing and exhaust-fan effects; see the outside air step.
  • If the chimney exits through the wall 7 feet (2.1m) or less above the ground, enclose it in a chase.
  • Fit a radiation shield at the ceiling/roof that runs completely through the cavity to the outermost plane of the roof; trim it flush if needed for the flashing.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of the floor, walls and ceiling/roof.
  • Minimum chimney 8'; minimum ceiling clearance 7'.
Using only the 8' minimum of chimney can give dirtier glass than 12' of chimney.
Refractory bricks
Before the first fire: rear brick, then the right and left sides, soft insulation on the floor, the bottom brick, then the two front bricks. No modifications needed.

The soft insulation fits tight between the front and back bricks and between the two side bricks. Figure 21 identifies which brick is left and which is right at each step. To remove a brick, reverse the sequence.

panels.title: Smoke spills when the door opens
items: Door opened too fast → open slowly, let the pressure stabilize
Dirty chimney or plugged cap (screened caps clog with creosote)
Chimney too short for the altitude and elbows → Table 4
Blower running → switch it off before opening the door
Range hood or bath fan running → crack a window near the fireplace
Too little kindling: smoke is most likely while lighting

panels.title: Burns too fast, won't slow down
items: Air leaking at door seals or gaskets → paper test, replace
Hole in a secondary air tube at the top of the firebox
Air control has no effect → leak, likely the door gasket; stop using
Excessive draft → hotter fire, shorter burns, less heat recovered
Chimney connector behind the top louver glowing red = over-firing

panels.title: Weak draft
items: Smoke entering the room; hard to light or operate
Often wrongly blamed on a blocked air intake
Most common fix: add chimney height (Table 4)
Cold outside chimney → enclose it in an insulated chase

panels.title: Smoldering fire or dirty glass
items: Air closed too far or too fast → reopen, wait, close gradually
Wet wood → excess visible smoke, dark deposits on the glass
Wax fire logs dirty the glass
Fire not hot enough: a hot fire once a day cleans most deposits
8' minimum chimney may give dirtier glass than 12'

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Open the combustion air control all the way first (lever fully to the right). The fire needs as much air as possible to get going.

Top-down start (recommended)

  1. Behind the front bricks, criss-cross 2-3 layers of small wood: about 10 pieces, 1" to 2" in diameter.
  2. Criss-cross about 20 finger-sized pieces of kindling on top, then add a few pieces of paper.
  3. Light the top of the pile. Close the door most of the way, but not completely. You should see air rushing in.
  4. After about 2 minutes, close the door. If the fire wants to smolder, crack it open for another minute or two. The taller your chimney and the colder it is outside, the longer it needs.
  5. When the start-up fuel is a nice coal bed, rake the coals forward and add up to 6 logs: bottom layer front to back, next layer left to right.
  6. Keep the door cracked a couple of minutes while the logs catch, then close it. Leave the air control on maximum until the next reload.

Prefer the traditional way? Crumpled paper under 3 or 4 criss-crossed layers of kindling, with the door kept about 1" from closed.

Never use flammable liquids or a grate, and never leave the fire burning with the door open or ajar. Keep the fire behind the front step, and put logs back if they fall against the glass.

air.title: Using the air controls
air.html:
Your fireplace has no chimney damper. The closed door seals the system, and two controls decide how much air the fire gets and where it comes from.

Combustion air control: the burn rate

  • Lever all the way to the right lets in the most air. Moving it to the left lets in less.
  • It gets hot enough to burn you. Use the handle or gloves provided.
  • Close it gradually, never from maximum to minimum at once. If the fire starts to smolder, open it again and wait longer before cutting back.
  • Always keep visible flame; it keeps the glass and chimney clean. In some homes the control can't close fully and still hold a fire. That's normal.

Outside air control: where the air comes from

It's a shutter behind the bottom louver. Lift the louver trim slightly and pull it off to reach the lever. Facing forward is open to outside air; pointing up is closed (room air). If your fireplace is connected to outside air, keep it open while burning. Close it when it isn't connected, when it isn't burning, and over the summer.

If moving the air control doesn't change the burn rate, air is leaking in, most likely at the door gasket. Stop using the fireplace until the leak is fixed.

reload.title: Reloading the fire
reload.html:
1. Have the next load ready before you open the door. The firebox cools while the door is open, but don't rush.
  2. Turn off the blower, if you have one. A running fan can push smoke out of the fireplace.
  3. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill into the room.
  4. Poke and stir the unburnt wood to revive the fire, then add the new logs. Keep a clear path in front of the "pilot": the metal air tube centered between the two andiron posts. It brings air to the coals.
  5. Leave the door slightly ajar for a couple of minutes until the new wood is well lit, then close it and set the air control to suit you.
  6. Wait about 20 minutes before turning the blower back on.

Heat vs. burn time

A faster fire makes more heat, but it burns more wood and sends more heat up the chimney. If it's burning too quickly, turn the air down. If it smolders with no visible flame, turn the air up.

Smoke spilling in? Make sure kitchen and bathroom fans are off. They create negative pressure that pulls smoke out of the fireplace.

firstfire.title: Your first few fires
firstfire.html:
The first few fires behave a little differently. Here's what's normal.

A slow start

The refractory bricks lining the firebox hold moisture from manufacturing, and it takes a few hot fires to dry them out. Until then they look black with smoke deposits. Once the moisture is gone, they turn white.

No break-in needed

Unlike cast iron stoves, this fireplace doesn't need curing with small fires first. Feel free to light a large fire from the very start.

A slight odor

You'll smell paint curing and oil burning off the metal. It may be strong enough to set off your smoke detector. Open doors and windows to air out the room.

Before the very first fire, make sure the refractory bricks are properly installed inside the firebox.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
This fireplace burns best on seasoned cordwood: wood that's been cut, split and dried under cover for at least 6 months, preferably a year or more. Dry seasoned wood is generally under 20% moisture. A wood moisture meter takes the guesswork out.

  • Wet wood is hard to burn, gives little heat, builds up creosote and darkens the glass.
  • Hardwoods burn longer and more evenly, because more weight fits in the firebox.
  • Never burn driftwood, treated wood, coal, garbage, plastic or scrap. Don't use construction scraps (2x4 or plywood) as your only fuel.
  • Large amounts of paper, cardboard, mill ends or construction waste can over-fire the fireplace, or start a chimney fire if the flue is dirty.

Fire logs

Densified fuel logs are fine, alone or mixed with wood. Wax fire logs (like Duraflame) aren't recommended because they dirty the glass. If you use one anyway, burn only one at a time and don't poke or stir it. Use only firelogs evaluated for fireplace use, and read the package warnings first.

glass.title: Glass & ash cleanup
glass.html:
Glass

A good hot fire once a day usually burns off most deposits. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass.

  • Light buildup: dampen a ball of newspaper, dip it in the fireplace ashes to make a paste, scrub, then wipe clean.
  • Heavier buildup: use a woodstove glass cleaner your dealer recommends.
  • Never clean the glass while it's hot, and never use an abrasive cleaner unless it's made for the job.
  • Heat won't break the 5mm ceramic glass, but a knock can.

Ashes

Take ashes out before they're deep enough to spill when you open the door. Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid, set on a non-combustible floor or the ground, well away from anything that burns. If you bury or spread them, keep them in the closed container until all cinders have cooled. The removable ash lip at the front keeps ashes from piling up there; its rear edge goes behind the firebox's vertical lip.

Paint

Wipe painted surfaces with a soft damp cloth, mild detergent and water. No abrasive cleaners, and don't spray glass cleaner on the paint.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
A slow-burning fire makes tar and vapors that condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If creosote catches fire, it burns extremely hot.

  • Check the chimney for creosote every week or so until you learn how often yours needs cleaning.
  • Clean it once buildup reaches 1/8" (3 mm), before more accumulates. Soot or creosote thicker than 1/8" (3 mm) means the chimney needs immediate cleaning. It may also mean you need to change how you burn and inspect the chimney more often.
  • Dry wood and a fire with visible flame help keep the chimney clean.

Sweeping

  1. Remove the baffle, the hard insulation panel above the tubes at the top of the firebox: take out the front burn tube, then slide the baffle forward and out through the door opening.
  2. Close the fireplace door.
  3. Remove the chimney cap and sweep with a 6" round soft-bristle brush.
  4. Put the baffle and tube back the same way. The tube's holes face slightly upward; insert its locking pin.
A chimney cap with a screen is more likely to clog with creosote. If your chimney has a flexible stainless-steel liner, take care not to dislodge it while cleaning.

door.title: Door seal & gasket
door.html:
A good door seal is the most important thing for controlling the burn rate. A poorly adjusted door can mean lower efficiency, over-firing, excessive wood use and early failure of the fireplace.

The paper test

  1. Put a sheet of paper between the door and the front of the fireplace, and latch the door.
  2. Pull gently but firmly. If you feel resistance, the seal is good.
  3. Repeat along all sides of the door.

Time for a new gasket?

Gaskets wear over time. If it's getting hard to slow the fire down, or burns are getting shorter, the gasket may be letting air in. Replacement kits (part code FO-GRK5) are available from your RSF dealer.

The manual also prints FO-GRK8 for the gasket kit (p. 5); p. 21 and the options list on p. 29 give FO-GRK5.

The latch pin and hinges can be adjusted (shown as diagrams in the manual). The door should seal when latched without being hard to close; over-tightening wears the gasket early. Don't slam the door, or the glass can break.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• Burn with the door fully closed. A partly open door can draw gas and flame out of the fireplace.
  • Keep furniture, firewood and other combustibles at least 4' from the front.
  • Have at least one smoke detector on each level of your home, and at least one carbon monoxide detector.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire, and keep them well away while it's in use.
  • Don't use a grate, don't tamper with the air control or add a flue damper, and don't install an insert or a gas log set.
  • The air control, bottom louver trim and outside air lever can get hot enough to burn. Use the handle or gloves provided.

Signs of over-firing

Don't over-fire the fireplace. You're over-firing if you can't slow the burn rate down, or if the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red. Over-firing can damage the fireplace, and that damage isn't covered by the warranty. If it burns excessively fast, check the door seal and have the secondary air tubes at the top of the firebox inspected for holes.

Carbon monoxide: burning wood produces smoke and CO, a poisonous gas. Keep the door gasket sealing properly and the chimney joints in good condition.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
RSF warrants its wood-burning fireplaces against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years, on these terms:

First yeardefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Years 2–5defective parts repaired or replaced; no labor
Years 6–30replacement parts, if available, at 50% of published retail price; no labor
Electrical componentsone year only

Not covered

  • Glass, plating and andirons
  • Normal wear: paint discoloration, worn gaskets, eroded or cracked refractory
  • Damage from vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or fuel loads, or skipped service
  • Installations that don't follow the manual, and damage in transit
  • Repairs not authorized by RSF in advance

The warranty isn't transferable. Defective parts are handled through an authorized RSF dealer, and RSF doesn't pay freight on replacement parts. Use only genuine RSF parts; substitutes void the warranty.

This is a summary. The full terms and exclusions are in the official PDF.

specOutput.title: Output, efficiency & emissions
specOutput.html:

Weighted average EPA efficiency70% (higher heating value)

Maker's website: BTU Maximum 50,000 BTU/h - Based on engineering calculations using firebox volume, efficiency, loading density (12lb/cu ft for hardwood), average humidity, reloading interval, type of installation, etc.

Efficiencies use CSA B415.1:22 calculations; the 75.3% figure is under the best burning conditions. Suitable for manufactured / mobile homes, solid fuel only.

Certified by UL (listing mark for Canada and U.S., file MH61405), tested to CAN/ULC-S610, CAN/ULC-S627 and UL 127. The listing label is glued to the bottom of the fireplace below the floor shield; remove the bottom louver to see it.

review.notes: Wood-burning unit: no gas, ignition system or gas-smell block; lighting is by hand (the manual recommends a top-down fire). Not stated in the manual's text, so not used and not checked against the catalog: unit dimensions and weight (Figure 1 is a drawing), firebox volume, maximum log length, glass/viewing size, heating area, non-catalytic design, the 2.04 / 1.6 cu ft firebox figures. Framing dimensions (Figure 4, p. 9) extract as scrambled numbers, so the guide points to the drawing only. Figure 1 (p. 6) side-standoff dimension extracts as '81/8”'; written as 8 1/8" in the guide. Figure 17 (p. 17) labels the masonry adaptor both 'FO-FDM7' and 'FO-FDM6'; the text (p. 17) and options list (p. 29) give FO-FDM6, which the guide uses. The listing paragraph (p. 4) and the visible-smoke paragraph (p. 25) call the unit an 'Insert', although it is a factory-built fireplace and p. 3 says not to install an insert in it. p. 25 calls the blower an 'inline blower'; elsewhere it is the 'internal blower'. The options list (p. 29) has an 'Electricity Required' column; the extract shows a mark only beside FO-HB9, so the guide only points to p. 29. Diagram-only content not transcribed: door latch and hinge adjustment (Figures 27-28), tube removal detail (Figure 26, shows 5/16"), minimum facing size (Figure 9), cement-board screw zone (Figure 8), refractory brick identification (Figure 21), outside-air control positions (Figure 24; the text's forward = open / upward = closed is used). p. 19 says the provided 5" x 36" spark guard 'can be cut to the minimum width' of 36" (Table 1 I); reads oddly but left as printed. The refueling text calls the air tube between the andiron posts the 'pilot'; the owner drawer explains it is an air tube. Warranty years shown as 'Years 2–5' and 'Years 6–30' for the manual's 'second through fifth' and 'sixth through thirtieth'. The card value 'g/h' abbreviates the manual's 'grams per hour'.
